## Where This Fits
The first week of Part III. For ten weeks every line of the compute ledger has been written in FLOPs. This week adds the two units that were missing — **bytes and bytes per second** — and folds the ledger into one picture, the roofline. Last week ended on the question of what each generated token costs in time and memory.

The week asks seven questions. **First, is the time spent computing or spent moving data?** An operation performs some number of FLOPs for every byte it reads from memory (its arithmetic intensity). The hardware, for its part, can perform a certain number of FLOPs in the time it takes to deliver one byte (peak compute divided by memory bandwidth). Comparing the two tells us which side the operation is stuck on. Prefill processes the whole prompt at once: the weights are read once and used thousands of times, so it is limited by compute. Decode emits one token per step, yet each step reads every weight and this sequence's entire KV cache, so it is limited by bandwidth. W3 set up the formula; this week puts numbers into it. A table published by Apple is a ready-made natural experiment: on the same models, moving from the M4 to the M5 made the wait for the first token 3.3–4.1 times shorter, while each later token arrived only 19–27% faster — and the memory bandwidth of the two chips differs by a factor of 1.28. (This is a company blog post, not a paper, and it measures the base M5, not the machine used in class.)

**Second, one formula with four knobs.** Once the intensity of decode is written as a single expression, the inference optimisations of 2023–2026 can be sorted by the knob each one turns: run several sequences in one batch (the weights are read once and shared); store each weight in fewer bits (quantization); shrink the per-sequence KV cache (GQA, MLA, KV quantization, eviction, sparse attention); verify several tokens in one pass (speculative decoding). Replacing the model by a smaller one (distillation) shrinks every term together. The same expression gives two boundaries. With a short context, the batch has to reach tens or even a hundred sequences before decode stops being bandwidth-bound. With a long context, the per-sequence KV cache cannot be shared across sequences, and no batch size gets decode out of that regime.

**Third, assembling the batch is the serving system's job.** Users do not arrive together and do not finish together. Iteration-level scheduling (later known as continuous batching) lets requests join and leave at every step. PagedAttention manages KV-cache memory with the paging idea from operating systems, and its argument is clean enough to finish on a blackboard. Chunked prefill keeps one long prompt from stalling everyone who is already generating. Prefill and decode are placed on different machines because on the roofline they were two different points all along. What is measured is not throughput but throughput *within the latency targets*.

**Fourth, a speed-up that leaves the output distribution unchanged.** In speculative decoding a small model drafts a few tokens and the large model checks them in one pass. The acceptance rule is designed so that the final distribution is **exactly** what the large model would have sampled on its own — a three-line proof, done in full on the blackboard. When the method stops paying off is decided by the expression from the second question.

**Fifth, a speed-up paid for in precision: quantization.** Weights go from 16 bits to about 4; fewer bytes are moved, while the arithmetic is still done in 16 bits. How to do it — which values are outliers, whether to look at the weights or at the activations, whether to quantize after training or during it — is a literature of its own, and below 4 bits is a different world. Whether a low-precision format can be *computed with* directly depends on whether the hardware has it. Inference optimisation is tied to hardware, and the formats the classroom machine lacks are themselves teaching material.

**Sixth, the costs that the usual metric does not show — this week's failure cases.** A score that barely moves after compression does not mean that behaviour is unchanged. The number of correct answers can stay the same while a different set of questions is answered correctly (NeurIPS 2024). After KV eviction, some instructions in a multi-instruction prompt are silently ignored and the system prompt becomes easier to extract (ACL 2026, the second half of this week's reading). The answer can still be right while the reasoning that supports it no longer does (Findings of EMNLP 2026) — the other half of last week's conflict between efficiency and monitorability. Even "the same request at temperature 0" does not guarantee the same output: the request is merged into batches of different sizes, and the order of summation inside the kernels changes with the batch (an experiment in a company blog post, and an oral paper at NeurIPS 2025).

**Seventh, simply use a smaller model.** Distillation moves cost from inference back to training; the on-policy distillation announced in W9 is taken up here. The week closes by giving every line of the ledger its unit and placing all of them on one roofline. **The measurement of the two roofs, the ten lines of speculative sampling with the sweep over the draft length, and the "same score, different behaviour" experiment are run by the instructor on the demo machine.** Students run nothing. That machine has no CUDA, so vLLM and FP8/NVFP4 cannot run on it — which is part of this week's argument.

## Learning Objectives
1. Define arithmetic intensity and the ridge point, write the lower bound on the time of one step, $t \ge \max(\text{bytes}/\text{BW},\ \text{FLOPs}/F_{\max})$, and say on which side of the roofline prefill and decode each fall. Compute $I^{*}$ for the demo machine from two numbers: its memory bandwidth and its measured peak FLOP/s.
2. Write the intensity of decode, $I(B, L, \gamma)$, and name the class of methods behind each of its four knobs (batching, weight quantization, the five ways of shrinking the KV cache, speculative decoding). Derive the two boundaries: the batch size $B^{*}$ at which a short-context decode stops being bandwidth-bound, and the context length $L_c$ beyond which no batch size gets it out.
3. Say which concrete problem each of the following solves: iteration-level scheduling (continuous batching), PagedAttention, chunked prefill, and prefill–decode disaggregation. Restate the memory argument of PagedAttention (three kinds of waste, and the bound after paging). Describe a serving target in terms of TTFT, TPOT and goodput.
4. Prove in three lines that speculative sampling produces exactly the target model's distribution, explain why the per-token acceptance probability is $\sum_x \min(p(x), q(x))$, and compare it with the scheme that accepts a draft token only when both models sample the same token (neither changes the distribution; their acceptance rates differ).
5. Derive the expected number of tokens per round of speculative decoding and the resulting speed-up, and optimise over the draft length $\gamma$. State where the assumption behind the formula (one verification pass costs about one decode step) fails, and why the conclusion "useless at large batch" reverses for long contexts.
6. Explain that weight-only quantization saves bytes rather than FLOPs, how the error of uniform quantization depends on outliers, and what GPTQ and AWQ each look at. Compare post-training quantization, quantization-aware training and low-precision training, and say which number formats need hardware support.
7. Give three failures that the usual metric does not show (answer flips; instructions ignored and system prompts leaked under KV eviction; answers that stay right while their evidence does not), and name the measurement that reveals each. Explain why temperature 0 is still not deterministic (kernels are not batch-invariant) and why reasoning models amplify the effect.
8. Place LoRA, MoE, quantization, KV compression and distillation in one table according to what each reduces (parameter count, bytes per weight, FLOPs per token, training memory, or per-sequence state), and say where distillation moves the cost.

## References
- **Textbooks**: **no textbook chapter covers this week.** None of the 26 chapter titles of JM3 (release of 2026-08-19) concerns inference efficiency, quantization or serving (the section level was not checked one by one); §7.6 *Decoding*, cited last week, is the prerequisite for speculative decoding. The material for this week is the papers below and the instructor's notes.

**Computing or moving: the roofline**
- Williams, Waterman & Patterson, **Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures**, *Communications of the ACM* 52(4), 65–76 (2009) — the source of the roofline model; defines arithmetic intensity and the ridge point
- Yuan et al., **LLM Inference Unveiled: Survey and Roofline Model Insights**, arXiv:2402.16363 (2024) — organises LLM inference techniques with the roofline model; **preprint**
- Patel et al., **Splitwise: Efficient Generative LLM Inference Using Phase Splitting**, ISCA 2024 (arXiv:2311.18677) — the abstract: prompt computation is compute-intensive and token generation memory-intensive; the two phases run on separate machines
- Sadhukhan et al., **Kinetics: Rethinking Test-Time Scaling Laws**, NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2506.05333) — cited last week; counting memory access changes the conclusions about test-time scaling
- Apple, **Exploring LLMs with MLX and the Neural Accelerators in the M5 GPU**, a **blog post** on Apple Machine Learning Research, 2025-11-19 (<https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/exploring-llms-mlx-m5>) — **a company post, not peer-reviewed**; M5 against M4 on six models: time to first token 3.33–4.06 times faster, generation 1.19–1.27 times faster, memory bandwidth 153 against 120 GB/s; **the base M5, not the classroom machine**
- Apple, **Apple debuts M5 Pro and M5 Max to supercharge the most demanding pro workflows**, an Apple **press release**, 2026-03-03 (<https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2026/03/apple-debuts-m5-pro-and-m5-max-to-supercharge-the-most-demanding-pro-workflows/>) — **a vendor specification, not a measurement**; unified memory bandwidth of the M5 Max "up to 614GB/s", the figure used in this week's blackboard calculation

**The KV cache: shrinking the per-sequence state**
- Ainslie et al., **GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints**, EMNLP 2023 (arXiv:2305.13245) — covered in W3; changes $n_{\text{kv}}$
- DeepSeek-AI, **DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Model**, arXiv:2405.04434 (2024) — MLA (W3); **a technical report**
- Liu et al., **KIVI: A Tuning-Free Asymmetric 2bit Quantization for KV Cache**, ICML 2024 (arXiv:2402.02750) — the abstract: keys are quantized per channel and values per token; at 2 bits quality is almost unchanged and peak memory, weights included, drops 2.6-fold
- Hooper et al., **KVQuant: Towards 10 Million Context Length LLM Inference with KV Cache Quantization**, NeurIPS 2024 (arXiv:2401.18079) — one of the four techniques in the abstract is to quantize keys **before** RoPE
- Zhang et al., **H$_2$O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle for Efficient Generative Inference of Large Language Models**, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2306.14048) — the representative KV-eviction method (W5)
- Xiao et al., **Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2309.17453) — StreamingLLM (W5, demo 4); used again in this week's demo 3
- Yuan et al., **Native Sparse Attention: Hardware-Aligned and Natively Trainable Sparse Attention**, ACL 2025 (arXiv:2502.11089) — each query reads only $k$ selected keys, and the model is trained that way (W5)
- Łańcucki et al., **Inference-Time Hyper-Scaling with KV Cache Compression**, NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2506.05345) — cited last week; the abstract: generation cost is bottlenecked by the size of the KV cache; a sparsification trained for 1K steps reaches 8× compression
- Li et al., **A Survey on Large Language Model Acceleration based on KV Cache Management**, TMLR 2025 (arXiv:2412.19442) — a map of the area
- Jiang et al., **Towards Efficient Large Language Model Serving: A Survey on System-Aware KV Cache Optimization**, Findings of ACL 2026 (arXiv:2607.08057) — a survey of the KV cache from the serving system's side

**Serving systems: assembling the batch**
- Yu et al., **Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models**, OSDI 2022, pp. 521–538 (USENIX; **no arXiv version**) — iteration-level scheduling, the origin of what is now called continuous batching
- Kwon et al., **Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention**, SOSP 2023 (arXiv:2309.06180) — **the origin of vLLM and the source of this week's blackboard argument**; existing systems used only 20.4%–38.2% of KV-cache memory for token states; the abstract: 2–4× throughput
- Agrawal et al., **Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference with Sarathi-Serve**, OSDI 2024 (arXiv:2403.02310) — chunked prefills and stall-free scheduling; preceded by Agrawal et al., **SARATHI: Efficient LLM Inference by Piggybacking Decodes with Chunked Prefills**, arXiv:2308.16369 (2023, preprint)
- Zhong et al., **DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized Large Language Model Serving**, OSDI 2024 (arXiv:2401.09670) — prefill and decode on different GPUs; the source of goodput as the metric
- Qin et al., **Mooncake: A KVCache-centric Disaggregated Architecture for LLM Serving**, arXiv:2407.00079 (2024; conference version at FAST 2025, journal version in *ACM Transactions on Storage* 22, 2026) — treats the KV cache as something to store and reuse across requests; the serving platform behind Kimi
- Zheng et al., **SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs**, NeurIPS 2024 (arXiv:2312.07104) — another widely used serving system; reuse of prefix KV caches
- Li et al., **Reasoning Language Model Inference Serving Unveiled: An Empirical Study**, ICLR 2026 (arXiv:2510.18672) — continues last week; the abstract: serving reasoning models shows large memory fluctuations and straggler requests; quantization and speculative decoding help, while prefix caching and KV-cache quantization may hurt small reasoning models
- Zhen et al., **Taming the Titans: A Survey of Efficient LLM Inference Serving**, INLG 2025 (arXiv:2504.19720) — a map of serving systems
- The vLLM project documentation (<https://docs.vllm.ai>) — **documentation, not a paper**; design changes made after the 2023 paper are described in the documentation and in engineering blog posts, and should be cited as such

**Speculative decoding**
- Leviathan, Kalman & Matias, **Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding**, ICML 2023, oral (arXiv:2211.17192) — **assigned reading this week (in full)**; the proof that the distribution is unchanged (Appendix A.1), the acceptance rate (§3.2) and the speed-up (Theorem 3.8)
- Chen et al., **Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling**, arXiv:2302.01318 (2023) — the same idea, proposed independently at about the same time; **preprint**
- Sun et al., **SpecTr: Fast Speculative Decoding via Optimal Transport**, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2310.15141) — casts the acceptance rule as optimal transport (a generalisation of maximal coupling) and extends it to several candidates per position
- Cai et al., **Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads**, ICML 2024 (arXiv:2401.10774) — no separate draft model: extra heads on the target predict several later tokens at once
- Li et al., **EAGLE: Speculative Sampling Requires Rethinking Feature Uncertainty**, ICML 2024 (arXiv:2401.15077); **EAGLE-2: Faster Inference of Language Models with Dynamic Draft Trees**, EMNLP 2024 (arXiv:2406.16858); **EAGLE-3: Scaling up Inference Acceleration of Large Language Models via Training-Time Test**, NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2503.01840) — the line of trained draft heads; **in class only the idea that the draft can be a small head on the target**
- Zhang et al., **Draft & Verify: Lossless Large Language Model Acceleration via Self-Speculative Decoding**, ACL 2024 (arXiv:2309.08168) — the abstract: drafting skips some of the target's own intermediate layers; the full model then verifies
- Fu et al., **Break the Sequential Dependency of LLM Inference Using Lookahead Decoding**, ICML 2024 (arXiv:2402.02057) — another exact parallel decoding scheme with no draft model; the first sentence of its abstract is that decoding is bounded by memory bandwidth
- Su, Giannoula & Pekhimenko, **The Synergy of Speculative Decoding and Batching in Serving Large Language Models**, arXiv:2310.18813 (2023) — the abstract: the optimal speculation length depends on the batch size; **preprint**
- Sadhukhan et al., **MagicDec: Breaking the Latency-Throughput Tradeoff for Long Context Generation with Speculative Decoding**, ICLR 2025 (arXiv:2408.11049) — **the counterexample to "useless at large batch"**; the abstract: for moderate to long sequences, up to 2.51× speed-up at batch sizes from 32 to 256
- Abramovich et al., **SPEED-Bench: A Unified and Diverse Benchmark for Speculative Decoding**, ICML 2026 (arXiv:2604.09557) — the abstract: synthetic inputs overestimate real-world throughput; the optimal draft length depends on the batch size
- Zhang et al., **Correctness Forensics for Batch Speculative Decoding: Diagnosing the Ragged Tensor Problem**, Findings of EMNLP 2026 (arXiv:2510.22876) — **a case of the "unchanged distribution" broken by the implementation**; the abstract: several widely used batched implementations silently produce corrupted output, invisible when only throughput is measured
- Ranjan et al., **Why Speculative Decoding Works Better Than Predicted on Sparse MoE Models**, NeurIPS 2026 (arXiv:2610.38981) — speculative decoding on MoE models; the abstract: across ten sparse MoE models, fine-grained ones depart from the prediction based on expert saturation
- Kumar, Dao & May, **Speculative Speculative Decoding**, ICLR 2026 (arXiv:2603.03251) — drafts the next round while verification is still running; one example of how this line is still moving in 2026
- Kim et al., **EfficientRollout: System-Aware Self-Speculative Decoding for RL Rollouts**, NeurIPS 2026 (arXiv:2606.18967) — continues W9: the sampling half of RL is decoding; the abstract: as the active batch shrinks, decoding moves from compute-bound back to memory-bound, and speculation is switched on only then

**Quantization**
- Dettmers et al., **LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale**, NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv:2208.07339) — an early method that treats outlier features separately in higher precision
- Frantar et al., **GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers**, ICLR 2023 (arXiv:2210.17323) — one-shot, layer-by-layer weight quantization using approximate second-order information
- Lin et al., **AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration**, MLSys 2024, best paper (arXiv:2306.00978; the conference title adds the word *On-Device*) — the abstract: which weights matter is decided by the activations, not the weights; protecting 1% of them greatly reduces the error
- Xiao et al., **SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models**, ICML 2023 (arXiv:2211.10438) — 8-bit weights and 8-bit activations (W8A8); migrates the activation outliers to the weight side
- Dettmers & Zettlemoyer, **The case for 4-bit precision: k-bit Inference Scaling Laws**, ICML 2023 (arXiv:2212.09720) — the abstract: at a fixed total number of model bits, 4-bit precision is almost universally optimal
- Kumar et al., **Scaling Laws for Precision**, ICLR 2025, oral (arXiv:2411.04330) — cited in W7; the abstract: the degradation from post-training quantization grows with the amount of training data
- Zhou et al., **From Signal Degradation to Computation Collapse: Uncovering the Two Failure Modes of LLM Quantization**, Findings of ACL 2026 (arXiv:2604.19884) — the abstract: 4-bit and 2-bit quantization fail in different ways — the first degrades the signal, the second stops key components from functioning
- Wang et al., **BitNet: Scaling 1-bit Transformers for Large Language Models**, arXiv:2310.11453 (2023); Ma et al., **The Era of 1-bit LLMs: All Large Language Models are in 1.58 Bits**, arXiv:2402.17764 (2024); Ma et al., **BitNet b1.58 2B4T Technical Report**, arXiv:2504.12285 (2025) — trained with ternary weights from the start; the third describes a downloadable 2B model; **all three are preprints or technical reports**
- Wang et al., **CAT-Q: Cost-efficient and Accurate Ternary Quantization for LLMs**, ICML 2026, oral (arXiv:2606.26650) — the abstract: post-training quantization to ternary weights from 512 calibration samples — the claim that anything below 2 bits must be trained from scratch is moving
- Castro et al., **Quartet: Native FP4 Training Can Be Optimal for Large Language Models**, NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2505.14669) — training end to end in 4-bit floating point; relies on a Blackwell hardware format and **cannot run on the classroom machine**
- NVIDIA, **Pretraining Large Language Models with NVFP4**, arXiv:2509.25149 (2025) — the abstract: a 12B model trained on 10 trillion tokens, with loss and downstream accuracy comparable to an FP8 baseline; **a company technical report**
- Rouhani et al., **Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning**, arXiv:2310.10537 (2023) — the source of the MX block floating-point formats (MXFP4, MXFP8); **preprint**

**Costs the usual metric does not show**
- Chen et al., **The Pitfalls of KV Cache Compression**, ACL 2026 (arXiv:2510.00231) — **assigned reading this week (§3–§4), and the central text for this week's failure cases**; five KV-eviction methods on two models; some instructions are in effect ignored altogether, and system-prompt leakage rises with compression
- Dutta et al., **Accuracy is Not All You Need**, NeurIPS 2024 (arXiv:2407.09141) — the abstract: when accuracy before and after compression is close, answers still flip between correct and incorrect in bulk; argues for reporting distance metrics as well
- Ai, He & Guo, **Does Accuracy Equal Evidence? Reasoning Faithfulness under KV Cache Compression**, Findings of EMNLP 2026 (arXiv:2608.01631) — continues last week; the abstract: eviction methods keep final-answer accuracy while the supporting reasoning chain no longer holds; a quantization control is much less affected
- Haverbeck et al., **The risk of KV cache compression**, NeurIPS 2026 (arXiv:2607.01520) — theory: once attention can sharply retrieve individual tokens, compression cannot uniformly beat random sampling without information about future queries
- von Rad, Cao & Geiger, **UniComp: A Unified Evaluation of Large Language Model Compression via Pruning, Quantization, and Distillation**, EMNLP 2026 (arXiv:2602.09130) — the abstract: after compression factual recall is largely preserved while multi-step reasoning, multilingual and instruction-following abilities degrade; retained performance does not imply preserved safety and fairness
- Ayadi et al., **Reliability Scaling Laws for Quantized Large Language Models**, TMLR 2026 (arXiv:2607.10855) — the abstract: performance scales monotonically with total bits, calibration and robustness do not; reliability peaks at 4 bits
- Zhou et al., **Instruction-Following Evaluation for Large Language Models**, arXiv:2311.07911 (2023) — IFEval: instructions that a program can check; used by Chen et al., and demo 3 writes a minimal version in the same spirit; **preprint**

**Determinism: after temperature 0**
- He et al., **Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference**, a **blog post** from Thinking Machines Lab, 2025-09-10 (<https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/defeating-nondeterminism-in-llm-inference/>) — **a company blog post, not a paper** (cited in W6); one prompt sent a thousand times gave 80 distinct outputs; the cause is that kernels are not batch-invariant
- Yuan et al., **Understanding and Mitigating Numerical Sources of Nondeterminism in LLM Inference**, NeurIPS 2025, oral (arXiv:2506.09501) — the abstract: under bf16 and greedy decoding, changing only the batch size and the number and type of GPUs moves a reasoning model's accuracy by up to 9% and its response length by 9,000 tokens
- Atil et al., **Non-Determinism of "Deterministic" LLM Settings**, arXiv:2408.04667 (2024; Eval4NLP 2025 workshop, under a slightly different title) — the same phenomenon measured from the API user's side; **a workshop paper**
- Pape, Evertz & Schönherr, **The Silent Hyperparameter: Quantifying the Impact of Inference Backends on LLM Reproducibility**, arXiv:2605.19537 (2026) — the abstract: with weights, decoding parameters and hardware fixed, changing only the inference backend shifts benchmark scores by up to 16.6 percentage points; **preprint**
- Kadadekar, **A Paired Testing Protocol for Batch-Conditioned Refusal Robustness in LLM Serving**, arXiv:2605.27763 (2026; an ICML 2026 workshop) — the abstract: the share of prompts whose refusal changes with the batch condition is small (about 0.16% after correction) and falls to zero with batch-invariant kernels; **a single-author workshop paper**

**A smaller model instead: distillation**
- Hinton, Vinyals & Dean, **Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network**, arXiv:1503.02531 (2015; NIPS 2014 Deep Learning Workshop) — the source of training a student on the teacher's whole output distribution, softened by a temperature
- Agarwal et al., **On-Policy Distillation of Language Models: Learning from Self-Generated Mistakes**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2306.13649); Gu et al., **MiniLLM: On-Policy Distillation of Large Language Models**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2306.08543) — cited in W9: the two academic sources of on-policy distillation
- Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, **On-Policy Distillation**, a Thinking Machines Lab **blog post**, 2025-10-27 (DOI 10.64434/tml.20251026) — **the widely circulated account; a blog post, not peer-reviewed** (cited in W9); it cites the two sources above itself
